walkthroughs.body_html: Asch (1951) showed participants a standard line and three comparison lines. Seven confederates gave the wrong answer first. The naive participant conformed on around 37% of critical trials, and 75% conformed at least once. Control error rate was under 1%, so the effect was group-driven.

Kelman (1958) distinguished compliance (shallow, public only), identification (moderate, tied to group role) and internalisation (deepest, public and private). Asch trials usually involve compliance; cult conversion is internalisation.

Deutsch & Gerard (1955) proposed two motives: NSI — fear of social rejection, leading to compliance — and ISI — wanting to be right in an ambiguous task, leading to internalisation. Ambiguous tasks tilt toward ISI; unambiguous public tasks like Asch tilt toward NSI.
